claims.text: The protective coating has a dual-phase FCC/BCC microstructure.
The FCC/BCC interphase boundaries in the starting coating are coherent and well defined.
Coexistence of the FCC and BCC phases forms coherent interphase boundaries.
Coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries act as effective dislocation-pinning sites.
Coherent FCC/BCC interfaces obstruct dislocation glide and time-dependent dislocation motion.
Interface-induced dislocation pinning limits the accumulation of plastic deformation over time.
Limiting time-dependent dislocation motion through coherent interfaces enhances creep resistance.
At elevated temperatures below the phase-destabilization threshold, the relevant microstructural characteristics remain intact during continuous-stress creep testing.
Coatings with intact, optimized FCC/BCC interfaces will have lower creep rates than coatings with deliberately disrupted interfaces under identical loading conditions.
Coatings with intact, optimized FCC/BCC interfaces will undergo less progressive plastic deformation than coatings with deliberately disrupted interfaces.
Poorly defined or intentionally altered FCC/BCC interfaces reduce dislocation-pinning effectiveness.
Coatings with poorly defined or altered FCC/BCC interfaces will exhibit higher creep strain under otherwise identical conditions.
Coatings with poorly defined or altered FCC/BCC interfaces will show an earlier onset of plastic deformation under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed protective mechanism operates only below limiting levels of applied stress and temperature.
Exceeding the stress or temperature stability limits can deteriorate the interphase boundaries.
Deterioration of the interphase boundaries leads to an increased creep rate.
Thermomechanical processing can intentionally disrupt the FCC/BCC interfaces for the proposed controlled comparison.
